title: Corporate mentions of Trump's tariffs spiked in spring 2025
gist: A PIIE text-analysis of 920 earnings calls from 150 US-listed companies (Jan 2025-Jul 2026) finds tariff mentions peaked at 85 percent of calls in Q2 2025 right after Trump's April 2 'Liberation Day' announcement and fell to 34 percent by Q2 2026, with average tariff passages per call dropping from six to one. The authors read this as habituation rather than relief, and warn that if Trump interprets fading corporate pushback as acquiescence he may escalate tariffs further.

themes.theme: Tariff-talk decay curve in earnings calls

insights.claim: US corporate executives mentioned tariffs in 85 percent of quarterly earnings calls in Q2 2025 (immediately after the April 2, 2025 'Liberation Day' announcement) but in only 34 percent of calls by Q2 2026, based on a sample of 920 calls from 150 companies.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Tariff commentary intensity is a tradable sentiment gauge: the 85 percent-to-34 percent collapse marks the point where trade policy stopped being a repricing catalyst for equities and became background noise.
insights.quote: We found that executives in 85 percent of calls in the sample mentioned tariffs during the second quarter of 2025, peaking in the wake of Trump's Liberation Day announcement.

insights.claim: The average number of passages mentioning tariffs per US earnings call fell from six in Q2 2025 to one in Q2 2026, a six-fold drop in narrative intensity over four quarters.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Intensity per call, not just incidence, has normalized - a signal that management guidance is no longer being built around trade-policy contingencies.
insights.quote: the average number of passages mentioning tariffs per earnings call dropped from six in the second quarter of 2025 to one in the second quarter of 2026

insights.claim: Corporate silence on tariffs should be read as habituation to a new policy norm rather than as evidence that tariff costs have disappeared, since firms may simply have adapted, grown less concerned, or judged that saying nothing is safest on a politically charged topic.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Do not treat falling tariff mentions as an all-clear on margins; the cost may have migrated from disclosed risk language into quietly repriced input costs and guidance.
insights.quote: Some may have decided that silence was the best way to navigate a politically charged topic.

insights.claim: The declining frequency of tariff discussion is interpreted by PIIE as evidence that firms now find White House trade policy less shocking than a year earlier, implying the shock component of tariff announcements has largely been discounted.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Event-driven tariff trades have decaying half-lives; the same announcement magnitude now moves less corporate language and probably less price.
insights.quote: These results suggest that firms find White House tariff policy less shocking now than a year ago.

themes.theme: Policy whipsaw after the Supreme Court ruling

insights.claim: The US Supreme Court struck down Trump's so-called reciprocal tariffs as unconstitutional in February, but the administration immediately replaced them with temporary tariffs that expired on July 24, and on that same day ordered new tariffs justified as combating forced labor.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Legal defeat did not lower the effective tariff wall - it only changed the statutory wrapper, so positioning for tariff relief on court outcomes has repeatedly failed.
insights.quote: He followed that ruling by announcing temporary tariffs that expired on July 24, the same day he ordered new tariffs that he said would combat forced labor.

insights.claim: US trade policy under Trump's second term has been delivered as successive waves of new tariffs on nearly all imports from almost all countries, surprising firms, financial markets, and governments alike.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Breadth (nearly all imports, almost all countries) means country- or sector-specific tariff hedges have limited value versus broad input-cost hedges.
insights.quote: He has surprised firms, financial markets, and governments by imposing successive waves of new tariffs on nearly all imports from almost all countries.
insights.locator: US trade policy remains unpredictable in President

insights.claim: Tariff discussion clusters in the industrials, materials, and consumer discretionary sectors, which depend on physical goods, while communication services, utilities, and real estate executives mention tariffs far less.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Confirms the goods-versus-services split as the cleanest axis for pairing long domestic-services exposure against tariff-exposed goods producers.
insights.quote: Executives in the industrials, materials, and consumer discretionary sectors mentioned tariffs the most, which is apt given their dependence on physical goods.
insights.locator: Mentions of tariffs by corporate leaders varied by sector

insights.claim: Every sector - including tariff-insulated service sectors such as utilities and real estate - showed a conspicuous peak in tariff mentions in the second quarter of 2025, indicating the April 2025 announcement produced an economy-wide attention shock rather than a goods-only one.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Correlated attention shocks across unrelated sectors argue the initial tariff repricing was a broad risk-premium event rather than a differentiated fundamental one - which is where cross-sector dispersion trades pay.
insights.quote: But mentions of tariffs in every sector conspicuously peaked in the second quarter of 2025.

insights.claim: Frank Sullivan, chair of US paint and coatings maker RPM International Inc., told a July 22, 2026 earnings call that he expects another volatile year and characterized the administration as one that seems not to like stability.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: A named specialty-coatings chair still guiding to policy volatility in mid-2026 shows goods-heavy managements are planning for continued disruption even as aggregate tariff chatter fades.
insights.quote: "Our guess is it's going to be another volatile year. We have an administration that seems to not like stability."

insights.claim: Contrary to the intuition that small caps should worry more about tariffs because they have weaker supplier-negotiating power and less ability to win exemptions, companies across the S&P 500, S&P MidCap 400, and S&P SmallCap 600 discussed tariffs in a similar pattern.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'small caps are the tariff-pain trade' thesis at the level of stated management concern - any size-based tariff spread has to be justified by realized margins, not by narrative.
insights.quote: But companies in the S&P 500, 400, and 600 behaved similarly, following the general pattern shown in the figure.

insights.claim: Larger companies have successfully lobbied for tariff exemptions, giving them a structural cost advantage over smaller firms that lack the same supplier-negotiating and exemption-seeking power.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Exemption access is an underappreciated moat: within the same tariff-exposed industry, scale converts political access into a gross-margin differential.

insights.claim: Falling corporate complaint about tariffs is itself a risk factor, because if Trump reads declining pushback as acquiescence he may raise tariffs further despite potential harms to businesses and consumers.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Sets up a reflexive loop worth hedging: the quieter earnings calls get on tariffs, the higher the implied probability of the next escalation should be priced.
insights.quote: If he sees declining corporate pushback as acquiescence, he could choose to raise tariffs further, despite potential harms to businesses and consumers.
insights.locator: Trump may deliver new tariff shocks

insights.claim: A renewed tariff escalation would be detectable early through a sharp rebound in tariff mentions on earnings calls, making transcript keyword frequency a usable leading indicator of policy shock absorption.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Build or buy a transcript keyword tracker: mention-rate reacceleration above the ~34 percent Q2 2026 baseline is a cheap early-warning trigger for trade-sensitive positioning.
insights.quote: Such a scenario should sharply increase mention of tariffs in future earnings calls.
insights.locator: Trump may deliver new tariff shocks in the months

insights.claim: The PIIE tariff-mention measure counts only company statements - analyst questions are dropped because they do not necessarily reflect company sentiment, though management answers to those questions are counted.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: Matters for anyone replicating the signal: including analyst questions would conflate sell-side curiosity with actual corporate exposure and likely overstate the persistence of tariff concern.
insights.quote: Questions raised during earnings calls are dropped because they do not necessarily reflect company sentiments; most come during Q&A sections of the calls and are made by sell-side equity analysts.

insights.claim: The choice to count 'passages' containing the word tariff is acknowledged by the authors as arbitrary, but a robustness check using total tariff word counts per call produced similar results.
insights.speaker: Gary Clyde Hufbauer
insights.so_what: The decay pattern survives a change of counting metric, so the fade in tariff attention is unlikely to be a measurement artifact.
insights.quote: A robustness check was run using total "tariff" word counts per call, with similar results.
